newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia gov't endorses sugar tariff removal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia gov't endorses sugar tariff removal.

text.p: The Australian federal and Queensland state governments on Wednesday endorsed a recommendation for the removal of an A$55 per tonne tariff on sugar imports effective June 30, 1997 and a call for anti-dumping measures to be strengthened.
Federal Primary Industries and Energy Minister John Anderson said the government supported the removal of the tariff, which was outlined in an industry working party paper on Wednesday.
"In the circumstances, the recommendations of the working party are likely to be accepted by the federal government, Anderson said in a statement.
The paper also urged the federal government to strengthen Australia's countervailing and anti-dumping laws "to provide appropriate protection for the sugar industry".

In recommending the tarif be scrapped, the review acknowledged the measure would likely result in a decline in raw sugar revenues of A$26.7 million but said it would ensure domestic refiners and industrial users have access to sugar at world market prices.

The tariff is currently imposed on all sugar imports into Australia, at a rate of A$55 a tonne. A developing country discount results in an effective tariff of about A$37 a tonne on raw sugar imports.
The review carries 74 recommendations in all, including a call for the retention of the Queensland Sugar Corp as the single desk seller of sugar for domestic and export markets.
The Queensland government has already endorsed the recommendations, Trevor Perrett, Queensland' Primary Industries minister said.

"The coalition (federal government) recognises the Queensland government's responsibility for the single desk export arrangements, and notes the review has the support of industry leaders, "Anderson said.

The paper said it found that the single desk selling system enables the Queensland sugar industry to influence regional price premiums by managing the export supply of raw sugar, which is worth between A$30 million and A$60 million a year to the industry.
But it said a complex pool price differential programme discriminated against some sectors of the industry and called for the practice to be cancelled.
The recommendations have won support from a wide cross-section of Australia's sugar industry although the changes are expected to cause some hardships, particularly to farmers.

"At a time when we are suffering a severe decline in world price, many growers will be adversely affected by the loss of the tariff and phasing-out of the price pooling differential," Harry Bonanno, chairman of the Canegrowers farmers organization.
Sugar users assert that the changes will not cause a surge in imported sugar.
"The changes will not mean that significant amounts of sugar will be imported," said Stuart Spencer, chief executive officer of of the Confectionery Manufacturers of Australasia Ltd.

"The major outcome will be of the working party's recommendations will be that Australian sugar refines and food processors will buy local sugar in line with the price paid by overseas buyers of Australian sugar," he said in a statement.
Australia currently exports about 85 percent of its sugar, the Australian Sugar Milling Council said.
Production of sugar in 1996/97 is on track to reach 5.3 million tonnes, according to figures from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics.
